content.overview: Safe elevated work starts before anyone climbs. The first decision is whether a ladder is the right access method for the task, location, duration, material being handled, and body position required. In cultivation spaces, narrow aisles, wet floors, rolling benches, hoses, fans, lights, ducting, and crop canopies can turn a routine reach into a fall exposure. The safest plan matches the access equipment to the job rather than forcing the job onto whatever ladder is nearby.

vocabulary.definition: The ladder, platform, stair, lift, or other means selected to reach and work at an elevated location.
The body and tool position a worker must maintain while completing the task, including reach and balance demands.
The maximum load assigned to equipment by its design or manufacturer, including the user and carried materials.

sections.title: Start with the task, not the ladder
sections.body: Define the work before selecting equipment: where the hands must be, how long the task lasts, whether both hands are needed, what tools or materials must move with the worker, and whether the worker would have to lean or twist to reach. A ladder is primarily access equipment and should not be treated as a substitute for a more stable working surface when the task requires sustained force, wide side-to-side reach, or handling that compromises balance. If the work cannot be done while maintaining stable contact and controlled posture, select a different access method or redesign the task.

sections.title: Match equipment to the environment
sections.body: Check the floor, aisle width, nearby doors and traffic, irrigation activity, obstructions, overhead equipment, and available setup space. Portable ladders must be used on stable and level surfaces unless secured or otherwise stabilized as permitted by the applicable standard. Do not create a makeshift height increase by placing a ladder on boxes, benches, pallets, or other improvised supports. Plan where tools and materials will be staged so carrying them does not interfere with safe climbing or balance.

sections.title: Build a stop-work decision
sections.body: A worker should be able to explain what would make the selected access method unacceptable before starting. Examples include unstable footing, a defective ladder, a blocked setup zone, an unmanageable load, unexpected traffic, or a task that requires overreaching. The correct response is to stop, change the setup, or escalate—not to compensate with speed, extra reach, or improvised support. This turns ladder safety from a memory rule into a repeatable task-planning habit.

workedExamples: A technician needs to inspect one sensor above shoulder height for less than a minute. A correctly selected and inspected step ladder on a clear level floor may be appropriate if the task can be completed without overreach.

A worker must secure several meters of trellis while repeatedly reaching laterally and using both hands. The task should be redesigned around a more stable work platform or different work method rather than prolonged side-reaching from a ladder.
commonMistakes: Choosing a ladder only because it is closest instead of checking whether the task and environment fit ladder use.
Treating a bench, tote, or pallet as a safe way to add height under a ladder.
Planning the climb but not planning where tools, materials, hoses, and pedestrian traffic will be controlled.
content.practicalApplication: Before any elevated cultivation task, complete a 60-second access-method check: define the work position, load, setup surface, traffic, surrounding equipment, and stop-work triggers. State why the selected equipment is appropriate and what condition would require a different method.
content.summary: Safe elevated work begins with selecting the correct access method for the real task and environment. Stable setup, controlled reach, manageable loads, and an explicit stop-work rule are more important than simply having a ladder available.
